issues.issue: The recital says the HELOC Seller's representations and the remedies for their breach will be assigned to the Issuer only "to the extent provided in the related Assignment Agreement," while Section 2.03 of the Sale and Servicing Agreement has the Depositor assign all of its right, title and interest in this Agreement to the Issuing Entity. Who may enforce the Section 7 representations, and against whom the sole-remedy clause runs, turns on which of these controls.

The "Free Writing Prospectus" is defined only by a date, with no issuer, subject matter or content identified, and the term is then never used in any operative provision. Its scope would have to be construed from outside the instrument.

The definitions cascade — undefined capitalized terms take their meaning from the Sale and Servicing Agreement, which in turn defers to Appendix A of an Indenture that is not part of this instrument. Terms used throughout Section 7 such as "Revolving Credit Loan Schedule," "Equity LTV" and "Note Insurer" are not defined anywhere in this Agreement.

The Acquisition Price is left blank ("$ * ___ plus $ * in accrued interest"), so the single most material price term of the sale is not stated in the writing. What the Purchaser owed under Section 2(c) cannot be determined from the document.

This defines the Custodial Agreement as being among the Depositor, HELOC Seller, Master Servicer, Indenture Trustee and LaSalle Bank as Custodian, while the Insurance and Indemnity Agreement defines the same document as among the Indenture Trustee, Depositor, Sponsor and LaSalle Bank as master servicer and custodian. The two descriptions of the same instrument do not match.

"Custodian" is defined as LaSalle Bank, yet Section 5(a) repeatedly refers to "the HELOC Seller's Custodian" as a place where Mortgage Files may be held. Whether that is the defined Custodian or some other bailee of EMC is not resolved.

The Cut-off Date is given as a bare calendar date while the Insurance and Indemnity Agreement defines it as the close of business on February 15, 2007. Section 4(a) allocates payments "due on or before the Cut-off Date," so the missing time of day has consequences.

"Deleted HELOC" is defined by reference to "Substitute HELOC," which is in turn defined as a loan substituted for a Deleted HELOC. The pair of definitions is circular and neither fixes the point at which a loan becomes deleted.

Due Date is keyed to a "Scheduled Payment" set forth in the Mortgage Note, but Section 7(hh) says Minimum Monthly Payments are due on the first day of each month and Section 7(uu)/(vv) compute payments by Billing Cycle. Which instrument fixes the Due Date for a revolving line is left unsettled.

"EMC Flow Loans" is defined by reference to "a flow loan purchase agreement" that is never identified by date or counterparty. Section 4(b) carves the Mortgages related to EMC Flow Loans out of the delivery accommodations, so the class of loans excluded cannot be identified from the writing.

The Cut-off Date Balance is fixed at $666,016,193, while Section 2(a) requires the aggregate outstanding balance to equal that figure yet also sweeps in "all additional balances resulting from related Draws" made after the Cut-off Date. The fixed figure and the open-ended balance cannot both measure what was sold.

"HELOCs: Any of the HELOCs that are identified as such on the Mortgage Loan Schedule" defines the term by itself. The definition is circular and throws the entire identification of the assets sold onto a schedule prepared by the seller.

"Mortgage" is limited to an instrument creating a lien on "an interest in an estate in fee simple in real property," yet Sections 7(k), 7(mm) and 7(zz) expressly contemplate HELOCs secured by leasehold estates and ground leases. Leasehold-secured loans cannot be squared with the fee-simple-only definition.

The Mortgage File is defined as the items in Exhibit 1, while Section 7(gg) warrants that the Mortgage File contains the documents listed in Section 2.01 of the Sale and Servicing Agreement. The two document lists are not the same, so what a complete Mortgage File is depends on which provision governs.

"Mortgage Rate: the annual rate of interest borne by a Mortgage Note as stated herein" — "herein" points to this Agreement, which states no rate, where "therein" (the Mortgage Note) was plainly meant. The error matters because Net Mortgage Rate is built on this definition.

Net Mortgage Rate is computed from the Servicing Fee Rate, Master Servicing Fee Rate and LPMI Fee, none of which is defined in this Agreement, and the defined term is then used nowhere in it. Its content can only be supplied from outside the instrument.

An Opinion of Counsel may be given by the HELOC Seller's own counsel and need only be acceptable to the Indenture Trustee and Securities Administrator, yet under Section 6(a) such an opinion relieves the Seller of recording and Section 2.05 of the Sale and Servicing Agreement requires opinions addressed to the Note Insurer as well. The Note Insurer's role in accepting the opinion is left unreconciled.

This defines "Purchase Price" for repurchases, but the Sale and Servicing Agreement (Sections 2.02, 2.03, 2.04) requires the Sponsor to repurchase at the "Repurchase Price," a differently defined amount. Which measure EMC owes on a repurchase of the same loan is left to be construed between the two agreements.

Clause (vii) requires a Substitute HELOC to "have a maximum Mortgage Rate determined in accordance with then current underwriting standards," without saying whose standards or as of when. The criterion sets no measurable ceiling and is the only one of the nine conditions with no fixed benchmark.

"Securities Act" is defined a second time here although the recitals already defined it to include the Commission's rules and regulations promulgated thereunder. The two definitions of the same term differ in scope.

"Value" is defined but appears nowhere else in the Agreement, while the loan-quality representations turn instead on LTV, CLTV and Equity LTV (Section 7(kkk)) and on appraisals under Sections 7(x) and 7(y). The orphan definition invites argument that it supplies the appraisal standard those provisions leave open.

The sale is conditioned on satisfaction of "the conditions set forth in Section 11 hereof," but Section 11 is Fees and Expenses; the conditions to closing are in Section 10, as Section 2(c) itself recites. The cross-reference is wrong on its face.

"the closing for the issuance of the Securities" uses a capitalized term that is nowhere defined in this Agreement, which defines only "Notes" and "Certificates." Whether Securities means both, or only the classes sold in the Public Offering, is unresolved.

This requires the Purchaser to pay the Acquisition Price and also to "deliver the Securities to the HELOC Seller," while the recitals say only that "[c]ertain Certificates will be transferred by the Purchaser to the HELOC Seller as partial consideration" and the Acquisition Price is defined as cash alone. What the Seller was entitled to receive at closing cannot be squared across the two.

This creates and names the "Mortgage Loan Schedule," yet a dozen representations in Section 7 (for example 7(h), 7(hh), 7(kk) and 7(uu)) warrant facts by reference to a "Revolving Credit Loan Schedule" that is defined nowhere. Whether the two are the same document has to be construed.

Each sentence ends with the trailing phrase "and all payments thereof," which duplicates or expands the entitlement to "scheduled payments" just granted without saying what further payments (prepayments, draws, recoveries) it captures. The line between the Seller's and the Purchaser's collections is left uncertain.

The closing sentence obliges the Seller to record "the Mortgage and intervening assignments, if any, and the assignment of the Security Instrument" within 180 days "unless such assignment is not required to be recorded under the terms set forth in Section 6(a)," but Section 6(a) excuses only assignments of the Security Instrument and says nothing about recording the Mortgage itself. The exception does not fit the duty it qualifies.

The paragraph recites that "the Master Servicer agrees that it will not" alter the MERS codes, but the Master Servicer is not a party to this Agreement, which is only between EMC and the Purchaser. A purported covenant by a stranger to the instrument is unenforceable as written.

The parties acknowledge that the HELOCs "will ultimately be assigned" to the Indenture Trustee "on the date hereof" — a future, indefinite word paired with a fixed present date. Section 4(b) describes the same transfer as occurring through the Issuer under the Sale and Servicing Agreement and the Indenture on the Closing Date.

This preserves the Purchaser's "rights to demand cure, repurchase, substitution or other relief as provided in this Agreement" notwithstanding any examination, while the closing paragraph of Section 7 makes cure, repurchase and substitution the "sole and exclusive remedy." What "other relief" survives the sole-remedy clause is left to be construed.

The Custodian is said to "acknowledge receipt of each HELOC," whereas Section 2.02(a) of the Sale and Servicing Agreement has the Custodian acknowledge receipt of the Mortgage File for each HELOC, without review. Whether the initial certification certifies receipt of the loan or merely of a file is a real difference.

The first sentence requires the Indenture Trustee or Custodian to review the Mortgage File items and certify that all documents have been executed, received and relate to the scheduled HELOCs; the last sentence says the Custodian is "under no duty or obligation to inspect, review or examine said documents." The two sentences of the same subsection cannot both be given effect.

"Material Defect" is defined here as a missing, unexecuted or unrelated document, while Section 2.02(a) of the Sale and Servicing Agreement defines the same term to include a document that "does not conform on its face to the review criteria specified in this Section." The same defined term carries two different scopes across the linked agreements.

The Seller must "correct or cure any such Material Defect within 90 days from the date of notice" and, failing that, must substitute or repurchase "within 90 days of the date of notice" — both periods run from the same notice date, so the repurchase deadline expires simultaneously with the cure period. The sequence of obligations is internally impossible as drafted.

This subsection directs what "the Indenture Trustee ... shall" do on any repurchase or substitution, but the Indenture Trustee is not a party to this Agreement, which is between EMC and the Purchaser alone. The release machinery for a Deleted HELOC therefore depends on the Sale and Servicing Agreement rather than on these words.

A failure to provide recording evidence or an Opinion of Counsel "shall be considered a Material Defect, and the provisions of Section 5(c) and (d) shall apply," but Section 5(c) is only the interim-certification provision and contains no cure, substitution or repurchase machinery. Which remedy the cross-reference triggers must be construed.

The subsection declares the conveyance to be "a sale" and expressly not a pledge, then in the same breath deems the Agreement a security agreement granting a first priority security interest if a court holds otherwise. The character of the conveyance — and what the Purchaser owns as against EMC's creditors — is left to be construed from these competing declarations.

The first clause is qualified "in all material respects" but the second warrants that "all information supplied by, on behalf of, or concerning the Mortgagor is true, accurate and complete" without any materiality or knowledge limit and without identifying whose information or supplied to whom. The reach of that unbounded second clause is the natural battleground for any loan-file misrepresentation claim.

The representation that "[t]he proceeds of the Revolving Credit Loan have been fully disbursed and there is no requirement for future advances thereunder" cannot be squared with Section 2(a), which sells "all additional balances resulting from related Draws," or with Section 7(xx), which warrants that every loan has a Draw Period of 5, 10 or 15 years. A revolving line by definition contemplates future advances.

This warrants that "upon recordation the Purchaser or its designee will be the owner of record of the Mortgage," while Sections 4(b) and 6(a) provide that assignments are recorded from the HELOC Seller to the Indenture Trustee, and 4(c) puts the Indenture Trustee's code on MERS. Who becomes owner of record is stated two different ways.

Compliance with predatory-lending and disclosure laws is warranted only "in all material respects," while Section 2.02(n) of the Insurance and Indemnity Agreement provides that a mortgagor's Truth-in-Lending claim conclusively constitutes notice of a breach of this Section 7 and that "[a]ny such breach shall be deemed material." The materiality qualifier here and the deeming provision there pull in opposite directions.

The same sentence warrants that the loan "is not delinquent in payment more than 29 days" and that "no payment has been 30 days delinquent during the preceding twelve month period." The two delinquency thresholds are stated one day apart and over different periods, leaving the permitted delinquency status uncertain.

The clause protects "the interests of the Trustee on behalf of the Noteholders and the Note Insurer" and requires modifications to be reflected in the "Revolving Credit Loan Schedule," but neither "the Trustee" (as against the Indenture Trustee or the Owner Trustee) nor the "Revolving Credit Loan Schedule" is a term defined in this Agreement. Both references have to be supplied from outside the words used.

The representation reaches only selection procedures "reasonably believed by the HELOC Seller to be adverse," making the seller's own belief the measure of the warranty. Adverse selection that EMC did not believe adverse would not breach it, a limit the surrounding absolute representations do not carry.

This permits a Mortgaged Property to be held "by leasehold for a term longer than the term of the related Mortgage," while Section 7(mm) requires that the remaining lease term not terminate less than ten years after the maturity date of the HELOC. The two provisions set different minimum lease terms for the same loans.

The clause addresses only "first lien" and "second lien" Revolving Credit Loans, although the transaction is defined throughout as covering "first and junior lien" HELOCs. On an expressio unius reading a third-lien or other junior-lien loan carries no security-agreement warranty at all.

The representation is introduced "with respect to each junior lien Revolving Credit Loan" but the operative promise runs only to "the mortgagee under the second lien Revolving Credit Loan." Whether junior liens other than second liens get the notice-and-cure protection is not resolved by the words used.

The mechanics'-lien exception is limited to liens "insured against by the title insurance policy referred to in (w) below," but clause (w) does not require a title policy for junior lien HELOCs that are Piggyback Loans of $200,000 or less. For those loans the carve-out has no referent.

"[T]o the best of the HELOC Seller's knowledge" is placed only before the litigation clause, leaving the statements about material damage, repair and condemnation absolute. Whether the knowledge qualifier reaches back over the earlier clauses of the same sentence is the classic question this drafting poses.

The junior-lien notice warranty applies only "where required or customary in the jurisdiction," a standard with no stated source and no benchmark for what is customary. Whether any given loan is covered by the representation cannot be determined from the provision.

The encroachment exception depends on the title insurance policy "referred to in clause (w) below," yet clause (w) excuses a policy entirely for junior lien Piggyback Loans of $200,000 or less and permits a mere lien search instead. For those loans the exception cross-references something that need not exist.

This warrants hazard insurance by an insurer "acceptable under the Fannie Mae Guides" and flood coverage meeting Federal Insurance Administration guidelines, while Section 7(z) warrants insurance from an insurer "acceptable to the HELOC Seller" in an amount measured by a different least-of-three flood formula. Two different insurance standards are warranted for the same properties.

The junior-lien title insurance carve-out turns on whether a loan is a "Piggyback Loan" with an initial principal amount of $200,000 or less, but "Piggyback Loan" is capitalized and defined nowhere in this Agreement. The class of loans excused from the title-policy requirement cannot be identified.

This requires an appraisal by a disinterested Qualified Appraiser satisfying Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Title XI of FIRREA, while Section 7(y) warrants only an appraisal "which conformed to the underwriting requirements of the originator." The two appraisal representations set different standards for the same file.

This warrants only that each appraisal "conformed to the underwriting requirements of the originator," whereas Section 7(x) warrants a Qualified Appraiser and compliance with FIRREA and the agency guides. Whether an originator-standard appraisal satisfies the pool's appraisal warranty depends on which clause controls.

This warrants insurance from "an insurer which is acceptable to the HELOC Seller" and flood coverage equal to the least of three amounts, while Section 7(v) requires an insurer acceptable under the Fannie Mae Guides and flood coverage meeting Federal Insurance Administration guidelines conforming to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac requirements. The same insurance is warranted twice on inconsistent terms.

Each HELOC is warranted to be a REMIC "qualified mortgage," but Section 2(a) sells lines of credit whose balances grow with post-closing Draws and Section 2.05(b) of the Sale and Servicing Agreement expressly contemplates discovery that a HELOC is not a qualified mortgage. The absolute warranty and the transaction's revolving structure sit uneasily together.

After a closed list of named statutes and labels, the clause sweeps in "a similarly classified loan using different terminology under a law imposing heightened regulatory scrutiny or additional legal liability." That catch-all has no boundary and would have to be read against the enumerated specifics that precede it.

The representation is made as to "Schedule A of the Prospectus Supplement," while this Agreement has its own Schedule A (Required Ratings for Each Class of Notes) and Section 5(d) refers to yet another Schedule A attached to the interim certification. Which Schedule A is warranted must be construed.

This fixes the Standard & Poor's LEVELS Glossary at "Version 5.6c, Appendix E, attached hereto as Exhibit 6," while Section 2.01(c)(v) of the Sale and Servicing Agreement identifies the very same Exhibit 6 to this Agreement as "Version 5.7 Revised." The two documents describe the same exhibit as two different versions of the test for a covered loan.

"[T]he underwriting guidelines of the related originator" are neither identified, attached, nor dated, and the clause admits no allowance for documented exceptions. What guidelines a loan had to satisfy is the central question in any origination-quality dispute and cannot be answered from the instrument.

Recordation is warranted "in accordance with the requirements of Section 2.01 of the Sale and Servicing Agreement," but Section 2.01(e) of that agreement requires assignments to be submitted for recording only upon a Recordation Event, whereas Section 6(a) of this Agreement imposes a flat 180-day recording deadline. The two recording regimes cannot both be the measure of this warranty.

The Mortgage File is warranted to contain the documents listed in Section 2.01 of the Sale and Servicing Agreement, while Section 1 of this Agreement defines the Mortgage File as the items referred to in Exhibit 1. The two lists are not identical, so the contents warranted depend on which definition governs.

This warrants that Minimum Monthly Payments "are due and payable on the first day of each month," while the Section 1 definition of Due Date makes the payment date whatever "the related Mortgage Note" specifies. The fixed first-of-the-month rule and the note-driven Due Date cannot both be right for every loan.

"Accepted Servicing Practices" is capitalized as a defined term but is not defined in this Agreement, and the servicing is performed under a separate Servicing Agreement not delivered with it. The standard against which servicing is warranted has to be found outside the instrument.

The clause turns on whether a loan is a "MERS Loan" recorded on the "MERS System," while Section 1 defines only the "MERS® System" and Section 4(c) speaks of HELOCs "registered on the MERS® System." It also warrants an Assignment acceptable for recording "other than with respect to the blank assignee," although Sections 4(b) and 6(a) contemplate assignments running to the Indenture Trustee.

The proviso that "no residence or dwelling is a single parcel of real property with a cooperative housing corporation erected thereon, or a mobile home" is garbled — a cooperative corporation is not something erected on a parcel — and it is unclear whether it excludes co-op units, co-op buildings, or neither. The mechanical defect changes what property types are warranted out of the pool.

The clause warrants that each prepayment penalty "is at least equal to the lesser of" the maximum permitted by law and six months' interest — a floor on the size of borrower penalties, where a purchaser protection would set a ceiling. Read literally it warrants that borrowers were charged the maximum lawful penalty, which cannot be reconciled with the predatory-lending compliance warranted in Section 7(e).

This requires that a lease not terminate less than ten years after the maturity date of the HELOC, while Section 7(zz)(ix) requires only that a ground lease term extend "at least five years beyond the maturity date of the related Revolving Credit Loan." A leasehold property can satisfy one and breach the other.

"[C]ustomary and enforceable provisions such as to render the rights and remedies of the holder thereof adequate" states no standard for what is customary or adequate and no jurisdiction by which to measure it. Whether a given mortgage form breaches the warranty is unanswerable on these words.

The exception for "any applicable security agreement or chattel mortgage referred to above" points back to Section 7(l), which addresses only first and second lien loans. For other junior lien loans the cross-reference has no content.

The warranty extends to any circumstance "that could reasonably be expected to cause investors to regard the Revolving Credit Loan as an unacceptable investment," without identifying which investors or what makes a loan unacceptable. That open-ended standard, unlike the specific bankruptcy statements beside it, has no boundary a court could apply without extrinsic evidence.

This warrants an adjustable "Mortgage Interest Rate" resetting monthly against an Index and Gross Margin, while Section 1 defines "Mortgage Rate" as "the annual rate of interest borne by a Mortgage Note" and builds Net Mortgage Rate on it. The Agreement uses two rate terms for the same loans without reconciling them.

"[E]ach Revolving Credit Loan requires the payment of a Cancellation Fee, where applicable" is self-cancelling: the qualifier "where applicable" removes any content from the warranty, and "Cancellation Fee" is nowhere defined. Nothing could breach it as written.

Every loan is warranted to have a term of 180 or 300 months and a Draw Period of 5, 10 or 15 years "followed by an Amortization Period of ten years." A 10-year Draw Period plus a 10-year Amortization Period is 240 months, which is neither of the two permitted terms, so the two sentences cannot both hold.

Clause (ix) requires the ground lease term to run "at least five years beyond the maturity date" of the loan, while Section 7(mm) requires that a lease not terminate less than ten years after maturity. The two leasehold warranties set incompatible minimum terms.

Condominium and PUD eligibility is measured by the "HELOC Seller's eligibility requirements as set forth in HELOC Seller's Underwriting Standards," a capitalized term defined nowhere, while Section 7(ee) measures origination by "the underwriting guidelines of the related originator." EMC did not originate these loans, so the two standards point to different documents.

The clause warrants that "no claims will arise as to broker fees that are double charged" — a promise about future third-party conduct rather than a statement of existing fact, made as of the Closing Date. What breach of a warranty about future claims would look like is left open.

The proviso caps lost note affidavits at "no more than 1% of the Revolving Credit Loans, in the aggregate," while Section 4(b)(iii) permits the Seller to deliver lost note affidavits in lieu of Mortgage Notes for every loan identified on Exhibit 5, without any percentage limit. The delivery accommodation and the warranty cap conflict.

This warrants that the Mortgage Note, Mortgage, Assignment and Exhibit 1 documents "have been delivered to the Purchaser or its designee," while Section 4(b) requires delivery to the Indenture Trustee or the Custodian on its behalf. Whether delivery to the Custodian satisfies a warranty of delivery to the Purchaser has to be construed.

The warranty that no "solid wastes" exist on any Mortgaged Property, as that term is defined in RCRA, is literally breached by ordinary household refuse on any residential lot. The absolute, unqualified scope of the term is what a court would be asked to cabin.

This repeats the disclosure warranty already made in Section 7(rr) and adds a forward-looking duty that "[t]he Servicer shall maintain such statement in the Servicing File," although the Servicer is not a party to this Agreement. The overlap with 7(rr) and the covenant on a non-party leave its operative effect unclear.

The warranty turns on "LTV," "CLTV" and "Equity LTV," none of which is defined in this Agreement, and the Section 1 definition of "Value" (the lesser of appraised value and sales price) is never tied to them. The ratios warranted cannot be computed from the instrument.

For second lien loans the Seller warrants it has received no "notice of default of a junior lien," although a second lienholder's exposure is to default under the senior lien, as Section 7(s)(3) recognizes by referring to encumbrances "senior to each Mortgage." "Junior" appears to be an error for "senior," and as written the warranty protects nothing.

"[N]o Mortgagor was encouraged or required to select" a higher-cost product uses an unmeasurable verb — what counts as encouragement by a loan officer is nowhere fixed — and the exception turns on "debit-to-income ratios," a misspelling of debt-to-income. The scope of the steering warranty cannot be determined from the words.

The warranty that underwriting "confirmed that at the time of origination, the Mortgagor had a reasonable ability to make timely payments" states no benchmark — no ratio, no documentation standard, no period over which ability is measured. On a stated-income revolving line that phrase is the whole battleground.

"[N]o Revolving Credit Loan is subject to negative amortization" cannot be squared with Section 7(w), which requires each title policy to contain "all applicable endorsements including a negative amortization endorsement, if applicable." If no loan negatively amortizes, the endorsement requirement is inexplicable.

The Seller warrants that "the Servicer has fully furnished ... accurate and complete information" to the three repositories on a monthly basis, although the Servicer is a non-party (GreenPoint) whose conduct EMC does not control, and no period is stated over which the monthly reporting is warranted. Both the actor and the time frame are left open.

The representations are said to inure to the Purchaser "its successors and assigns," while the sole-remedy paragraph that follows names only the Purchaser, the Indenture Trustee and the Noteholders and the Insurance and Indemnity Agreement makes the Note Insurer a third-party beneficiary of the Operative Documents. Whether the Note Insurer takes the benefit of these warranties as an assign is left to be construed across the documents.

The trigger states two different thresholds in one sentence: a breach "which materially and adversely affects the value of the interests of the Purchaser, the Noteholders, the Indenture Trustee or the Note Insurer ... or which adversely affects the interests of the Note Insurer." Whether the Note Insurer must show materiality at all, having been named in both limbs, is squarely presented by the words.

Cure, repurchase or substitution is made "the sole and exclusive remedy," yet Section 2.02(n) of the Insurance and Indemnity Agreement independently obliges the Sponsor to defend and indemnify the Insurer against all losses arising from the same breach of this Section 7. Whether the sole-remedy clause caps the Insurer's recovery under the Insurance Agreement is the central relational question of this transaction.

The provision defers accrual of a cause of action until discovery of the breach and a failure to cure, repurchase or substitute, although the representations themselves are made "as of the Closing Date" and are either true or false then. Whether parties can postpone accrual this way, and what "discovery" means, is exactly what such a clause invites a court to decide.

Paragraph (a) is a lead-in containing no representation and paragraph (b) begins the substance, so the lettering of the Section 8 warranties is displaced by one throughout. The section is also captioned "Concerning the HELOC Seller" here while the table of contents calls it "Concerning EMC."

The exception ends "and, in connection with the recordation of the Mortgages, powers of attorney or assignments of Mortgages not yet completed" — a dangling phrase with no verb, so what is being excepted from the no-consents representation is not stated. The mechanical incompleteness changes the reach of the warranty.

The second limb reaches only proceedings which "in the judgment of the HELOC Seller" could reasonably be expected to be determined adversely, making the seller's own judgment the measure of its disclosure obligation. Nothing in the clause fixes an objective standard against which that judgment could be tested.

"HELOC Seller's Information" is said to be defined in Section 13(a), the indemnification section, while Exhibit 3 to this Agreement is itself titled "HELOC Seller's Information." Which text fixes the scope of the information warranted has to be resolved between the two.

The disclosure of threatened proceedings is limited to those which "in the judgment of the Purchaser" could reasonably be expected to be determined adversely, leaving the Purchaser to set the threshold of its own warranty. No objective benchmark is supplied.

"Purchaser's Information" is said to be defined in Section 13(b), the indemnification section, while Exhibit 4 to this Agreement is separately titled "Purchaser's Information." The two possible sources of the definition are not reconciled.

This makes the Purchaser's obligations subject to the conditions "set forth in Section 10," but Section 2(a) conditions the purchase and sale on "the conditions set forth in Section 11 hereof" while Section 2(c) refers to Section 10. Which section states the conditions to closing is stated inconsistently across the Agreement.

The condition requires the Purchaser to have received "all of the following closing documents," but no list of documents follows the colon in the instrument, and the forms need only be "agreed upon and reasonably acceptable to the Purchaser." As written, neither the documents nor the standard for their sufficiency can be identified.
